Where to go from here?

  • By necessity, a class like this can only scratch the surface.

  • But our goals here are to put you in a good position to be able to:

    • be a critical consumer of other people’s research

    • be positioned to produce your own, if you choose to.

Where to go from here?

Some of the advice in these slides and the textbook chapter will be useful for your final paper, but not all of it:

  • You don’t need to include citations unless you are using outside materials. So you don’t need a literature review, and you don’t need to rely on journal articles if you do cite things.

  • Your intended audience for the paper is non-academic, so your tone can be more relaxed and less formal.

  • You’re somewhat limited in your options for research design and you’re not collecting data. You can take some creative liberties in framing and interpretation that might not be appropriate in other settings.

Reading research

Finding it

If you’re interested in “reading the literature” you’ve got to find it first.

  • For more informal research questions, check out major newspaper sources, reputable blogs, and think tanks (that aren’t totally nuts).

  • Peer reviewed scholarly journals are great sources, but locating good stuff can be tricky.

Finding Academic Research

  • You can add the UMD library reload button to access journals offline and then try Google scholar.

  • Or databases for GVPT students at the UMD library

  • However, these might be a little overwhelming for a narrow question.

Finding Academic Research

Alternative strategy that I find helpful:

  1. Look for an edited volume (example) or review article (example) on your topic

  2. Check the author and look for researchers discussed prominently in the text.

  3. Search for those authors and look for their personal or university websites, or their Google scholar page.

  4. Find their most recent research in your area of interest. Read them, and take note of papers cited in their literature review. Repeat step 3.

  • Since good research tries to build cumulative knowledge, reading the literature reviews in newer articles is a good way to know what’s really worth your time.

Reading an article

  • Once you’ve got a collection of papers you want to review, then next step is reading.

  • Pay attention to the methods, but don’t get too bogged down in the details. Good research will usually highlight the implications/interpretations of results.

Structure of an article

  • Abstract: briefly summarizes the article ahead.

  • Introduction: lays out the research question in more detail

    • This section will usually include a literature review that discusses existing findings from peer-reviewed literature.

    • It may include a separate theory section that details how the authors’ approach differs from prior work or the limits of existing knowledge on a topic

  • Methods: talks about the data collection strategy, measurement of the variables, and statistical models

  • Findings: shows the results of the statistical tests. Might include multiple robustness checks to anticipate potential critiques of the main result

  • Discussion/Conclusion: summarizes the findings again, discusses implications, and future work

Mining the abstract

A good place to start when looking at a journal article is with the abstract. You can use this as a roadmap that will tell you what ideas or findings are most important.

Mining the abstract

  • What is the research question/dependent variable?
  • What factors predict the outcome?
  • What is the unit of analysis/data source?
  • What do you expect to see? (good abstracts will spoil the ending!)

…We examine how individual donors and the mass public prioritize [judicial] nominations… To do so, we constructed original questions for a survey of over 7,000 validated donors and a comparison general population sample. We find donors are substantially more likely to prioritize nominations than their general public co-partisans, particularly Republican donors…

Canes-Wrone, Brandice, Jonathan P. Kastellec, and Nicolas Studen. “Mass Versus Donor Attitudes on the Importance of Supreme Court Nominations.” American Political Science Review (2025): 1-8. (link)

Questions to ask

When evaluating research, some key questions to ask are:

  • Does the operational definition match the theory? Are the hypotheses a logical extension of the argument?

  • What is the method for testing the hypothesis? How well does it address biases like confounding?

  • What are the results/conclusions/major takeaways?

  • How does this result fit with other research? How does it build on previous work? How might someone extend it?

Assessing research: methods sections

  • Especially for newer empirical research, there’s a very good chance that the methods section will contain a regression model, but it might include terminology or models you’ve never seen.

  • Really important stuff will usually be highlighted and interpreted in the text. Less prominent things (like alternate ways of calculating p-values) are probably not as crucial to understand.

  • When it doubt, ask around.

The tiny stuff at the bottom just means they’ve adjusted the standard errors to account for observations not being totally independent. This matters, but it doesn’t change how you interpret the results.

Assessing research: cause and effect

  • Identifying cause and effect relationships is one of the most challenging tasks in the social sciences. Its easy to say “this is how things are”, but its far harder to say “this is why this happens”.

Assessing research: cause and effect

  • In observational research, you should pay close attention to how/whether the researchers are addressing confounding variables: what else might explain the observed relationship between X and Y?

  • While there are some strategies for identifying cause and effect with observational data good researchers will usually be very cautious about interpreting things like a regression model as showing cause and effect.

  • In experiments, we’re less worried about confounding, but you should think about whether the result is externally valid (will it apply in the “real world”?)

  • Remember: we can manage random error by collecting more data, but bias will be a problem no matter how large the sample gets.

Assessing research: statistical significance and substantive significance

  • Statistical significance means that random sampling error probably doesn’t explain our results. It doesn’t mean a relationship is causal. Remember confounding.

  • Statistical significance doesn’t mean the relationship is important. At a large enough sample size, even very negligible effects are significant.

  • Statistical insignificance doesn’t mean that there’s no relationship: it means “we can’t rule out random chance”

Writing Research

Writing research: some (very) general steps

  • Formulate a question

  • Review prior work and proffer an explanation

  • Collect data and test a hypothesis

  • Write it up

Research questions

  • Good research questions often come up when you know stuff. So start by learning about a topic.

  • Not all questions are answerable even with really good data. Be strategic about what you’re asking.

  • Your research question should, at a minimum, imply what your dependent variable will be and hint at something you could test.

Reviewing prior work

(see previous advice on reading research)

  • Keep in mind: the goal here is to find out what is known and unknown so you can build on it.

  • You don’t need to read everything ever written on a topic. This may be unfeasible for broad topics, or even counterproductive (some stuff is low-quality)

Formulating an explanation

  • Brainstorm some ideas for what might explain the thing you’re researching.

  • Your theory doesn’t need to be completely novel! A lot of good research applies known theories to a new set of cases, or pits existing theories against each other.

  • What are some testable implications of this explanation? What are some alternative explanations that I would need to rule out?

Collecting data/Conduct analyses

  • (More information on finding data in the next section)

  • Document what you’re doing! Especially if you’re making changes that could impact your analysis.

  • Consider operational definitions: is your measurement a good “fit”?

  • Good theories will generate multiple hypotheses, and the best research will approach a question from multiple angles

Writing it up

Focus on the stuff that the reader needs to know to understand your analysis:

  • The reader probably doesn’t need to know that you used R. They probably do need to know things like: the wording and coding of survey questions, or the number of observations in your sample, or whether you used weights etc.

  • You don’t have to write things in the order they occur. It’s usually better to state your findings up front so the reader knows what to expect.

  • Explain your results. Explain what the reader should be seeing and use meaningful labels for things instead of variable names like polparty_3cat.

  • Talk about substantive implications of your findings.

  • Consider audience and genre: a blog post will probably have a very different tone from an academic article.

Conducting Research: being humble

  • Remember: science is a collective enterprise! Most things move forward incrementally, and a lot of great research is fairly intuitive (or looks that way after you read it)

  • Very few things worth studying can be proven with a single research paper. Acknowledge limitations and plausible rival explanations.

Technical stuff

Finding data

Some highlights

  • ANES data the NES data set in your workbook comes from the 2020 round, but this is a massive data set. There’s an R-package for downloading this, but if you want the latest rounds you’ll need to go to the website.

  • V-DEM is one of the sources of the variables in the world data set. They also have an R-package for downloading and interacting with the data.

  • Correlates of State Policy of data for state policy research. Also has an R-package.

Poliscidata

  • The author of the textbook maintains a big list of data sources that you can access for free at this link

Github

  • Github is primarily meant to manage code, but many people use it to host data.

  • For instance, you can check out the (sadly defunct) Github repository for Fivethirtyeight.com, which also has R code for replicating analyses from many of their articles.

Journal replication archives

Replication archives: many journals require authors to submit their code and data to a replication repository. Sometimes these are hosted on the journal’s website, but in many cases they’ll be hosted on the Harvard Dataverse

Dataverse pages for the top 3 political science journals:

  • Journal of Politics

  • American Political Science Review

  • American Journal of Political Science

Journal replication archives

  • In practice, not all replication code will work, and it won’t necessarily be written in R. (R code files will have a .R extension)

  • Contemporary political science uses a lot of methods not covered in this class!

]

Using a codebook

  • Most data sources will include a codebook that explains in detail what each variable means.

  • In many cases, you’ll need to reference this before you can make sense of any of the data.

Using a codebook

NES data, for instance, is basically unintelligible without looking up the code and values for each variable.

Using a codebook

  • In most cases, you’ll need to do a lot of recoding before you can start your analysis.

  • When you do this, be sure to document your steps in an R script so you can retrace your steps, re-use code, and share your work.

  • Don’t forget about weights! Large surveys like the NES typically have multiple weighting schemes. The codebook and user guide will usually tell you what to use and when.

Writing code

  • Be sure to write clear, annotated code that someone else could use to replicate, check, or modify your results.

  • Check and recheck your analyses, especially when doing things like re-coding data.

  • Make sure you can run things in order: you have to import the data before it can be used.

R coding

Suggestions for learning more about R coding:

  • Commands from RCPA3 are set up to help you avoid mistakes, but they’re slow and limited for a lot of applications, so I generally recommend looking for alternatives.

  • There are tons of resources for learning R programming available online. I recommend R For Data Science

  • Or try R bloggers, The Big Book of R or R for Political Science
